strengths: High-impact dataset for a critical domain: Tropical forests represent vital global biodiversity and carbon sinks, yet have been severely underrepresented in remote sensing benchmarks. SELVABOX provides over 83,000 expert-annotated tree crown bounding boxes across 14 orthomosaics in Brazil, Ecuador, and Panama, an order of magnitude larger than existing tropical forest datasets.

Rigorous data curation and protocol: Annotations were completed over 1,284 hours by domain experts (biologists) with systematic quality control, supplemented by photogrammetric Digital Surface Models (DSMs). The inclusion of spatially disjoint train/val/test splits prevents geospatial autocorrelation, and the AOI masking strategy effectively handles partially annotated regions.

Practitioner-oriented evaluation metric: The introduction of the RF1_75 raster-level metric addresses a crucial flaw in standard tile-level mAP evaluations, which fail to penalize edge artifacts and duplicate detections when aggregating back to whole-raster cartography.

Comprehensive benchmarking and strong empirical findings: The paper provides an extensive resolution and spatial extent ablation study, contrasting CNN baselines (Faster R-CNN, DeepForest, Detectree2) with modern vision transformers (DINO Swin-L). The multi-resolution data augmentation effectively bridges sensor resolution domain shifts.
High standard of reproducibility: The submission includes released data, preprocessed external benchmarks, code repositories, and two dedicated Python libraries under permissive open-source licenses.
weaknesses: Bounding box vs. instance segmentation annotations: While bounding boxes enable scaling to over 83k annotations, tropical tree crowns are frequently intertwined and irregular in shape. In dense canopies, bounding boxes often overlap significantly with neighboring crowns, where polygonal instance segmentation would provide finer delineation.

Absence of field-verified ground truth: Due to extreme logistical and geolocation challenges in dense neotropical forests, annotations rely solely on aerial photo-interpretation (RGB + photogrammetric elevation) without ground-stem validation, which may introduce systematic labeling biases for sub-canopy or intertwined trees.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The work primarily leverages existing vision architectures (DINO, Faster R-CNN) and standard data augmentation primitives (random cropping and resizing). The core contribution lies in the dataset, benchmark formulation, and evaluation protocol rather than novel model architectures.

NMS hyperparameter sensitivity for RF1_75: The RF1_75 score relies on tuning post-processing NMS thresholds (IoU threshold and confidence score) on the validation set for each dataset. While explored across thresholds in Section 5.3, an IoU-averaged raster metric (e.g., RF1_50:95) would provide an even more robust benchmark summary.

strengths: Significant dataset contribution addressing a major bottleneck in remote sensing and ecological AI: SelvaBox introduces >83,000 expert-annotated tropical tree crowns across three Neotropical countries (Brazil, Ecuador, Panama), providing an order of magnitude more annotations than all prior tropical tree crown datasets combined.

Methodologically sound dataset design and curation: The protocol incorporates domain-expert biologist annotators, DSM cross-referencing for canopy height disambiguation, explicit spatial splitting to prevent geospatial autocorrelation leakage, and an explicit pixel-masking mechanism to prevent penalizing models on sparsely annotated training regions.

Practitioner-oriented raster-level evaluation (RF1_75): The paper clearly articulates why tile-level metrics (e.g., standard COCO mAP on cropped tiles) fail due to boundary cuts and duplicates, introducing a principled raster-level evaluation after tiling aggregation and NMS matching.

Thorough and extensive benchmarking: The empirical study evaluates multiple architectures (CNN-based Faster R-CNN and RetinaNet vs. transformer-based DINO with Swin-L), explores spatial resolution vs. ground extent trade-offs, validates multi-resolution data augmentation, and conducts zero-shot out-of-distribution evaluation across five external benchmarks (both tropical and temperate/urban).

High reproducibility and practical tooling: In addition to publishing the data and pre-trained checkpoints under permissive open licenses, the authors provide modular open-source Python packages for tiling, georeferenced prediction aggregation, and standardized evaluation.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: The core machine learning components (DINO with Swin-L, standard multiscale cropping and resizing augmentation, NMS aggregation) are established off-the-shelf techniques rather than novel vision architectures designed specifically for dense forestry imagery.

Bounding boxes rather than instance segmentation masks: In dense, intertwined tropical canopies, axis-aligned bounding boxes inevitably contain substantial overlap and background foliage. Instance segmentation polygons (as in Detectree2 or QuebecTrees) provide significantly more accurate crown area and geometry estimates for downstream ecological modeling (e.g., allometric biomass estimation).

Sensitivity to inference post-processing hyperparameters: The raster-level RF1_75 metric depends substantially on tuning grid-searched NMS IoU and confidence thresholds (Tables 12–15 show wide variation across datasets, from 0.10 to 0.80 NMS IoU), which may limit fully automated deployment on uncalibrated test rasters.

Lack of ground-truthed field validation: Annotations rely solely on photo-interpretation supplemented by photogrammetric DSMs. While the authors appropriately discuss why ground surveys in dense tropical forests are logistically difficult and susceptible to GPS multipath errors, photo-interpretation in dense tropical canopies remains subject to observer bias and missed subcanopy trees.

strengths: High-impact dataset contribution: SELVABOX provides over 83,000 manually verified individual tree crown annotations across 14 orthomosaics in Brazil, Ecuador, and Panama, representing an order of magnitude increase in scale over existing open-access tropical forest datasets.

Rigorous annotation and spatial split methodology: Annotations were produced and cross-checked by five trained biologists (1,284 person-hours) with photogrammetric elevation data support; splits are strictly spatially separated to prevent geospatial auto-correlation, and sparse regions are systematically masked to avoid penalizing detectors on unlabeled trees.

Comprehensive benchmarking and insights: The paper conducts extensive evaluations across model paradigms (CNNs vs. Vision Transformers), multiple input resolutions (4.5, 6, 10 cm/px), and ground extents (40m vs. 80m), demonstrating the clear benefits of high resolution and Swin-L DINO architectures.

Practical multi-resolution augmentation and strong OOD generalization: The proposed multi-resolution cropping/resizing pipeline achieves scale-invariance, enabling models trained on SELVABOX (or multi-dataset combinations) to achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot detection performance on out-of-distribution tropical (BCI50ha, Detectree2) and non-tropical benchmarks.

Sound operational evaluation metric: The introduction of the raster-level F1 score (RF1_75) directly addresses the boundary/tile-edge artifacts inherent to standard tile-level mAP evaluations, aligning benchmark evaluation with practical ecological surveying needs.
Excellent reproducibility and software tooling: Full code, preprocessed datasets, and two open-source Python packages for raster tiling, inference, and raster-level NMS aggregation are provided.
weaknesses: Limited to bounding box annotations: While bounding boxes are suitable for detection and tree counting, instance segmentation masks (polygons) are often preferred by ecologists to accurately measure crown area, asymmetry, and biomass.

Heavy reliance on post-processing threshold tuning: The RF1_75 metric involves optimizing both NMS IoU and score thresholds on a validation set (Tables 12–15), which fluctuate significantly across configurations; guidance or automated heuristics for selecting these thresholds in practical deployments without local ground truth remains limited.

Technical novelty of model architectures: The core modeling leverages existing standard object detection frameworks (DINO, Faster R-CNN, DeepForest) rather than proposing domain-specific neural architectural innovations (though the multi-resolution training scheme and raster-level benchmark are well-conceived).

strengths: Addresses a crucial data scarcity bottleneck in ecological computer vision: tropical forests represent major global biodiversity and carbon sinks but have been heavily underrepresented in high-resolution open-access benchmarks.

Substantial dataset scale and quality, featuring over 83,000 expert-annotated bounding boxes across three Neotropical countries (Brazil, Ecuador, and Panama) with diverse sensors, lighting, and canopy structures.

Rigorous experimental methodology, including spatially non-overlapping splits to prevent spatial autocorrelation, masking strategies for sparse annotation regions, and an extensive ablation across ground sampling distances (GSD) and spatial extents.
Introduction of the RF1_75 metric to address the limitations of tile-level evaluation metrics by measuring detection accuracy after full-raster reconstruction and Non-Maximum Suppression aggregation.

Thorough out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation on external datasets (BCI50ha, Detectree2, NeonTreeEvaluation, QuebecTrees, OAM-TCD), showing strong zero-shot generalization of models trained on SELVABOX and multi-resolution augmentations.
High reproducibility and engineering contribution with the release of the dataset, pretrained models, and two permissive open-source Python packages (geodataset and CanopyRS).
weaknesses: Annotations are restricted to 2D bounding boxes rather than oriented bounding boxes or instance segmentation masks, which can introduce background noise and overlap ambiguity in extremely dense, intertwined tropical canopies.

Technical and algorithmic novelty is relatively limited from a pure machine learning perspective, as the modeling relies on established detection frameworks (DINO, Faster R-CNN) combined with standard multi-scale cropping and resizing augmentations.

Annotations were produced via single-pass labeling by biologists without reporting inter-annotator agreement or consistency metrics (e.g., box IoU overlap between independent annotators on a shared subset).

The raster-level RF1_75 evaluation requires tuning NMS hyperparameters on validation sets, which partially softens the zero-shot generalization setting for datasets where validation rasters are utilized.

strengths: High-impact dataset contribution: SELVABOX provides over 83,000 manually annotated tree crowns across three biodiverse tropical countries (Brazil, Ecuador, Panama), substantially filling a critical geographic and ecological data gap in the Global South where tropical forests are severely underrepresented.

Rigorous experimental design and spatial validation: The paper carefully constructs spatially separated splits to avoid spatial autocorrelation artifacts, addresses incomplete annotation issues with clean AOI masking, and provides extensive ablation studies across spatial resolutions (GSD) and tile extents.

Methodological contribution for remote sensing evaluation: The introduction of the raster-level RF1_75 metric effectively bridges the gap between conventional tile-level COCO metrics (which suffer from edge duplicates and border clipping) and practical remote sensing inventory needs.

Thorough benchmarking and cross-domain generalization: The benchmark includes multiple modern detectors (Faster R-CNN, DeepForest, Detectree2, DINO with Swin-L), comprehensively validating multi-resolution domain augmentation and testing zero-shot generalization across external tropical and temperate datasets (BCI50ha, Detectree2, OAM-TCD, etc.).

Open-source releases: Releasing preprocessed standardized datasets, pre-trained weights, and two well-scoped Python libraries (geodataset and CanopyRS) under permissive licenses provides substantial value to both the computer vision and ecology communities.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: The machine learning methodology relies on existing standard architectures (DINO, Faster R-CNN) and standard multi-scale random cropping/resizing augmentations, making the contribution primarily dataset- and benchmark-centric.

Bounding box vs. instance segmentation: Individual tree crowns in dense, multi-layer tropical canopies have irregular, intertwined boundaries. Bounding box annotations capture significant background and overlapping neighboring canopy, whereas polygon delineation (instance segmentation) is often preferred in forest ecology applications.

Single-pass manual annotation without inter-annotator agreement: The dataset annotations were produced in a single pass without independent secondary verification or a reported inter-annotator agreement study (e.g., box IoU overlap between multiple annotators on a shared subset) to quantify annotation ambiguity in dense canopies.

Threshold sensitivity of RF1_75: While the 0.75 IoU threshold for RF1 is justified in the text to avoid overly permissive matches, analyzing the metric's sensitivity across a wider range of IoU thresholds (or reporting an integral/average RF1 across thresholds) would provide further insight into the stability of raster-level rankings.

strengths: Substantial and timely dataset contribution: SELVABOX provides over 83,000 manually annotated tree crowns across three neotropical countries (Brazil, Ecuador, Panama) on very high-resolution drone imagery (1.2–5.1 cm/px GSD). Given that tropical forests are ecologically critical yet severely underrepresented in computer vision remote sensing benchmarks, this dataset fills an important gap.

Rigorous experimental design and data splitting: The paper explicitly uses spatially separated train/val/test splits to eliminate geospatial autocorrelation artifacts, and provides an effective masking strategy to handle sparse/incomplete annotation areas without penalizing models unjustly.

Application-oriented evaluation framework (RF1_75): The authors rightly identify the discrepancy between tile-level metrics (mAP/mAR) and operational forest inventory needs, introducing a raster-level evaluation metric after spatial aggregation and NMS, supported by clear algorithmic formalization.

Extensive cross-dataset and multi-resolution benchmarking: The empirical study evaluates multiple architectures (Faster R-CNN, DeepForest, Detectree2, DINO with Swin-L) across various resolutions, spatial extents, and includes comprehensive zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) testing across five external benchmarks (BCI50ha, Detectree2, QuebecTrees, NeonTreeEvaluation, OAM-TCD).

High engineering reproducibility and tool release: The authors open-source two dedicated Python packages (`geodataset` for GIS raster tiling/aggregation and `CanopyRS` for training/benchmarking), enhancing the practical utility and reproducibility for both ML and ecology communities.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic and architectural novelty: The technical modeling relies entirely on standard, off-the-shelf detection frameworks (DINO, Faster R-CNN) with conventional multiscale crop/resize augmentations, rather than introducing new model components, geospatial-specific attention mechanisms, or losses tailored to the physical characteristics of dense forest canopies.

Axis-aligned bounding boxes instead of instance segmentation masks: In dense, overlapping, and interlocking tropical canopies, axis-aligned bounding boxes inevitably contain significant background, overlapping neighbor foliage, and empty canopy gaps. While bounding boxes reduce annotation overhead, instance segmentation masks or oriented bounding boxes would provide much higher ecological fidelity for crown delineation and biomass estimation.

Annotation quality control and inter-annotator consistency: As acknowledged in the limitations, the 83k annotations were produced in a single pass across six annotators without secondary consensus review or formal inter-annotator agreement metrics (e.g., Fleiss' kappa or mean IoU across independent annotations on a sample area), which may leave residual label noise and bias.

Heuristic dependency of raster-level metric: The proposed RF1_75 metric is sensitive to tile boundary buffer stripping (5%) and NMS threshold tuning (τ_nms, s_min). Grid searching NMS thresholds per validation set can confound true model detector capabilities with post-processing tuning, particularly when transferring to unseen domains.
